title: How Plants Drink Water
summary: How roots take in water, how it rises through the stem to the leaves, and why plants need water to make food and stay firm.
poll: A plant's roots are its most important part.

versions.title: How Plants Drink
versions.text:
A plant needs water. But it has no mouth. So how does it drink?

It drinks with its roots. The roots are in the soil. They drink from the soil. Each root has tiny hairs. The hairs help a lot.

Then it goes up the stem. The stem has thin tubes. They are like straws. The water goes up and up.

Next it gets to the leaves. The leaves have tiny holes. Some water goes out. It goes into the air. This pulls more water up.

Plants use water to make food. They need the sun, too. Water keeps it firm.

With no water, a plant will wilt. It droops. Give it a drink. Soon it stands up.

Date palms grow in Saudi Arabia. Their roots go deep. They find water far down.

versions.title: How Plants Drink
versions.text:
Plants need water to live. But a plant has no mouth. So how does it drink?

A plant drinks with its roots. The roots grow down in the soil. They soak up water from the soil. Each root has tiny hairs. The hairs help the root take in more water.

Next, the water moves up the stem. Inside the stem are thin tubes. They work like straws. The water climbs up the tubes, all the way to the top.

Then the water reaches the leaves. Leaves have tiny holes. You cannot see them. Some water slips out of the holes into the air. As it goes, it pulls more water up the stem.

Plants use water and sunlight to make their own food. Water also brings bits of food from the soil. It keeps the plant firm.

If a plant gets no water, it will wilt. Its leaves droop. Give it a drink, and soon it stands up again.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms grow in dry land. Their roots go very deep to find water.

versions.title: How a Plant Gets a Drink
versions.text:
Every plant needs water to stay alive. But plants do not have mouths. So how does a plant get a drink?

A plant drinks through its roots. The roots spread out under the soil. They soak up water that is stored in the soil. Each root is covered with tiny root hairs. These hairs give the root more space to take in water.

Next, the water travels up the stem. Inside the stem are thin tubes, like a bundle of drinking straws. The water climbs through these tubes to every part of the plant.

At last, the water reaches the leaves. Leaves have tiny holes that are too small to see. Some water escapes through these holes into the air. As it escapes, it pulls more water up from the roots.

Plants use water, air, and sunlight to make their own food. The water also carries minerals from the soil. It keeps the stem and leaves firm.

When a plant does not get enough water, it begins to wilt. Its leaves droop and go soft. If you water it in time, it will stand tall again.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms grow in hot, dry places. Their long roots reach deep under the ground to find water.

versions.title: How a Plant Gets a Drink
versions.text:
Every plant needs water. This is true for the smallest weed and the tallest tree. Yet plants have no mouths. So how does a plant take a drink?

The answer begins underground with the roots. Roots spread through the soil. They soak up water stored between grains of dirt. Each root is covered with thousands of tiny root hairs. These hairs give the root much more surface to take in water.

From the roots, water travels up the stem. Inside the stem are narrow tubes that work like a bundle of drinking straws. The water climbs through them to every branch and leaf.

When the water reaches the leaves, some of it escapes into the air through tiny holes. As this water leaves, it pulls more water up behind it. It is like a drink going up a straw.

Plants use water, air, and sunlight to make their own food. The water also carries minerals from the soil, and it keeps the stem and leaves firm.

When a plant does not get enough water, it starts to wilt. Its leaves droop and feel soft. If it gets water in time, it will usually recover.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms survive in hot, dry places because their long roots reach water deep underground.

versions.title: How Plants Drink Water
versions.text:
Every living plant needs water, from a tiny weed in a crack to a tall palm tree. Yet plants have no mouths to drink with. So how does water get inside a plant and reach every leaf?

The journey begins underground. Roots spread through the soil and absorb water stored between the grains of dirt. Each root is covered with thousands of tiny root hairs. These hairs add a lot of extra surface, so the root can take in much more water.

Water then travels up through the stem inside narrow tubes called xylem. You can think of the xylem as a bundle of thin drinking straws that runs from the roots to the leaves.

What pulls the water upward? The answer is in the leaves. Each leaf has tiny holes, too small to see. Water inside the leaf turns into vapor and escapes through these holes into the air. When water evaporates from a leaf, it tugs on the water behind it, so more water rises from the roots.

Plants use water, air, and sunlight to make their own food. The water also carries minerals from the soil, and it keeps stems and leaves firm.

When a plant does not get enough water, it begins to wilt, and its leaves droop. Given water in time, it usually recovers.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms grow well in dry land because their deep roots reach water far underground.

The journey begins underground, where roots spread through the soil and absorb water stored between tiny grains of dirt. Each root is covered with thousands of microscopic root hairs. These hairs add a great deal of extra surface, which allows the root to take in far more water than it could otherwise.

Next, the water travels upward through the stem inside narrow tubes called xylem. You can picture the xylem as a bundle of thin drinking straws that stretches from the roots to the leaves.

But what actually pulls the water upward? The answer lies in the leaves. Each leaf has tiny openings, too small to see without a microscope. Water inside the leaf turns into vapor and escapes through these openings into the air. As water evaporates from the leaf, it tugs on the water behind it, so more water rises from the roots, much like a drink rising through a straw.

Plants use water, air, and sunlight to make their own food. The water also carries minerals from the soil, and it keeps the stems and leaves firm and upright.

When a plant does not receive enough water, it begins to wilt, and its leaves droop. If it gets water in time, it usually recovers.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms thrive in dry regions because their deep roots reach water stored far underground.

versions.title: The Journey of Water in a Plant
versions.text:
Every living plant depends on water, from a small weed growing in a sidewalk crack to a towering palm tree in a desert oasis. Plants have no mouths, however. So how does water enter a plant and travel all the way to its highest leaf?

The journey begins underground, where roots spread through the soil and absorb the water that collects between tiny particles of dirt. Each root is covered with thousands of microscopic root hairs, which add an enormous amount of extra surface and allow the plant to collect far more water than a smooth root could.

From the roots, the water moves upward through the stem inside narrow tubes called xylem. The xylem works like a bundle of thin drinking straws that stretches continuously from the roots to the leaves, carrying water to every branch along the way.

What actually pulls the water upward? Surprisingly, the answer lies in the leaves. Each leaf contains tiny openings that are too small to see without a microscope. Water inside the leaf turns into vapor and escapes through these openings into the air. As water evaporates from the leaf, it tugs on the water behind it, so a steady stream rises from the roots, much like a drink rising through a straw.

Plants combine water, air, and sunlight to produce their own food. The water also delivers minerals from the soil, and it keeps the stems and leaves firm and upright.

When a plant does not receive enough water, it begins to wilt, and its leaves droop and soften. If it is watered in time, it usually recovers.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms flourish in dry regions because their deep roots reach water stored far underground.

versions.title: The Journey of Water in a Plant
versions.text:

The journey begins underground, where roots spread through the soil and absorb the moisture that collects between tiny particles of earth. From the roots, the water moves upward through the stem inside narrow tubes called xylem. The xylem functions like a bundle of slender drinking straws that stretches continuously from the roots to the leaves, delivering water to every branch along the way.

What actually pulls the water upward against gravity? Surprisingly, the explanation lies in the leaves. Each leaf contains tiny openings that are invisible without a microscope. Water inside the leaf changes into vapor and escapes through these openings into the surrounding air. As water evaporates from the leaf, it tugs on the water behind it, so a steady stream rises from the roots, much like a beverage rising through a straw.

versions.title: How Plants Drink Water
versions.text:
Every living plant depends on water, whether it is a modest weed pushing through a sidewalk crack or a towering palm tree in a desert oasis. Plants have no mouths, however, so scientists spent centuries investigating how water enters a plant and climbs all the way to its highest leaf.

The journey begins underground, where roots spread through the soil and absorb the moisture that collects between tiny particles of earth. Each root is covered with thousands of microscopic root hairs, which provide an enormous amount of additional surface and allow the plant to gather far more water than a smooth root could.

From the roots, water moves upward through the stem inside narrow tubes called xylem. These tubes function like a bundle of slender drinking straws stretching continuously from the roots to the leaves.

What actually pulls the water upward against gravity? Surprisingly, the explanation lies in the leaves, which contain tiny pores called stomata. Water inside the leaf changes into vapor and escapes through the stomata into the surrounding air, a process known as transpiration. Water molecules also cling tightly to one another, a property called cohesion. As a result, each molecule that evaporates tugs on the one behind it, so an unbroken column of water rises from the roots, much like a beverage rising through a straw.

You can observe this process by placing a stalk of celery in a glass of water mixed with food coloring. Within a day, colored streaks appear in the leaves, revealing the path the water followed.

Plants combine water, carbon dioxide from the air, and energy from sunlight to manufacture their own food through photosynthesis. The water also transports dissolved minerals from the soil, and it keeps the stems and leaves firm and upright.

When a plant does not receive enough water, it begins to wilt, and its leaves droop and soften, although it usually recovers if it is watered in time.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms flourish in arid regions because their extensive roots reach groundwater stored deep beneath the surface.

versions.title: The Hidden Journey of Water in Plants
versions.text:
Every living plant depends on water, whether it is an inconspicuous weed forcing its way through a sidewalk crack or a towering palm tree flourishing in a remote desert oasis. Because plants categorically possess no mouths through which to drink, botanists spent centuries carefully investigating precisely how water initially penetrates a plant and then manages to rise, sometimes traveling dozens of meters, all the way up to its topmost leaf.

This remarkable journey begins underground, where extensive roots spread through the surrounding soil and absorb the moisture that collects between tiny particles of earth. Each individual root remains covered with thousands of delicate root hairs, which together provide an enormous amount of extra absorbing surface area and consequently let the plant gather far more water than any similarly smooth root could ever hope to collect.

From these absorbing roots, water then travels upward through the plant's stem through narrow internal tubes called xylem, which work essentially like a bundle of slender drinking straws reaching continuously from the roots all the way to the farthest leaves. This chain of tubes carries water the entire length of the plant.

What precisely propels this water upward against the constant pull of gravity? The underlying explanation lies specifically within the leaves themselves, which contain countless microscopic pores called stomata. Water inside the leaf gradually turns into vapor and then escapes through these stomata into the surrounding air, a process scientists formally describe as transpiration. This happens because individual water molecules cling tightly to one another, a distinctive property formally identified as cohesion. Every single molecule that evaporates simultaneously tugs upon its neighboring molecule below. So an unbroken column of water consequently rises steadily from the roots, much like a drink rising smoothly through a straw.

You can personally observe this otherwise invisible biological process by placing a stalk of celery in a glass of water mixed deliberately with food coloring. Within about a single day, clearly colored streaks appear visibly within the leaves, thereby revealing the precise physical pathway that the colored water followed through the internal xylem during its continuous ascending journey.

Plants combine water, carbon dioxide from the air, and captured sunlight to make their own essential food through the complex process of photosynthesis. The absorbed water also carries dissolved mineral nutrients upward from the soil while maintaining the essential internal pressure that keeps stems and leaves firm and properly upright.

When a plant fails to receive adequate water over time, it gradually begins to wilt, and its leaves consequently droop and soften noticeably, although it typically recovers completely and quickly if it receives prompt subsequent watering.

In Saudi Arabia specifically, date palms flourish remarkably within extraordinarily arid conditions precisely because their extensive root systems reach deep enough to find groundwater stored far beneath the desert surface, and this extraordinary biological adaptation fundamentally explains why date palms have successfully sustained desert communities throughout the Arabian Peninsula for many thousands of consecutive years.

versions.title: The Hidden Journey of Water in Plants
versions.text:
Every single living plant fundamentally and unavoidably depends upon water for survival, whether it constitutes an inconspicuous weed forcing its determined way through a narrow sidewalk crack or a towering date palm tree flourishing improbably within a remote desert oasis. Because plants categorically possess no mouths whatsoever through which to drink in any conventional sense, botanists devoted entire successive centuries to systematically investigating precisely how water initially penetrates a plant's root system and subsequently manages to ascend, occasionally traveling a remarkable distance of dozens of meters vertically, all the way upward to its most distant uppermost leaf.

This remarkable physiological journey originates fundamentally underground, where extensive branching root systems spread continuously throughout the surrounding soil matrix and absorb the residual moisture that persistently accumulates between countless microscopic particles of earth. Each individual root remains densely covered with thousands upon thousands of delicate root hairs, which collectively provide an absolutely enormous quantity of additional absorptive surface area and consequently enable the plant to gather considerably more water overall than any comparably smooth, hairless root could conceivably ever hope to collect.

From these absorbing roots, water subsequently travels continuously upward through the plant's central stem via narrow specialized internal vessels formally termed xylem, which function essentially like a coordinated bundle of innumerable slender drinking straws extending continuously and uninterruptedly from the absorbing roots all the way to the plant's most distant, highest foliage.

What, precisely, propels this considerable volume of water relentlessly upward against the persistent, ever-present downward force of gravity? Remarkably, the underlying scientific explanation resides specifically and primarily within the leaves themselves, which contain countless microscopic pores formally termed stomata. Water contained physically within the leaf tissue transforms progressively into gaseous vapor and subsequently escapes outward through these stomata into the surrounding atmosphere, a fundamental physiological process that scientists formally and technically describe as transpiration. Because individual water molecules cling tenaciously and persistently to one another through intermolecular attraction, a distinctive physical property formally identified as cohesion, every single molecule that evaporates from the leaf surface simultaneously exerts a tugging force upon its neighboring molecule situated immediately below it, so an uninterrupted, continuous column of water consequently rises steadily and reliably from the absorbing roots, functioning much like a beverage ascending smoothly and continuously through a narrow drinking straw.

You can personally and directly observe this otherwise entirely invisible biological process by placing a single stalk of celery within a glass of water combined deliberately with ordinary food coloring. Within approximately a single twenty-four-hour day, distinctly colored streaks materialize visibly within the leaf structure itself, thereby conclusively revealing the precise physical pathway that the artificially colored water consistently followed through the internal xylem vessels during its continuous, uninterrupted upward journey.

Plants fundamentally and continuously combine absorbed water, atmospheric carbon dioxide, and captured solar radiant energy to manufacture their own essential nutritional sustenance through the remarkably complex biochemical process of photosynthesis. The absorbed water simultaneously transports dissolved mineral nutrients upward from the surrounding soil while also maintaining the essential internal hydraulic pressure that keeps stems and leaves structurally rigid, firm, and properly upright throughout the plant's life.

When any given plant fails to receive adequate water over a sustained period, it inevitably and progressively begins to wilt noticeably, and its leaves consequently droop and soften quite visibly, although it typically recovers completely and relatively rapidly provided it subsequently receives prompt, adequate irrigation before permanent damage occurs.

In Saudi Arabia specifically, date palms flourish remarkably and improbably within extraordinarily arid environmental conditions precisely because their extensive, deeply penetrating root systems manage to reach groundwater reserves stored far beneath the desert's sandy surface, and this extraordinary evolutionary biological adaptation fundamentally explains precisely why date palms have successfully and continuously sustained human desert communities throughout the entire Arabian Peninsula for many thousands of consecutive years of recorded history.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?

wrong.A: The article does not talk about shade.
wrong.C: Date palms are named at the end, but the article does not teach how to plant them.
wrong.D: The article does not compare the size of leaves.

The stem

The roots

wrong.B: The stem carries water up, but it does not take it from the soil.

They are able to live without any water at all.
Their wide leaves soak up rain straight from the air.
They are planted only next to rivers and lakes.
questions.why: The article says their deep roots reach water far underground, which other plants with short roots could not reach.

wrong.B: Every plant needs water, the article says.
wrong.C: The article does not say palm leaves soak up rain.
wrong.D: The article says they grow in dry land, not next to rivers.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: "Roots spread through the soil and absorb water." What does absorb mean?
options: Push away
Take in
Freeze
Pour out
questions.why: Roots take in water from the soil, so absorb means to take in or soak up.

wrong.A: Roots do not push water away; they bring it in.
wrong.C: Nothing in the sentence is about freezing.
wrong.D: Water does not pour out of the roots.

questions.stem: How is most of the article organized?
options: It compares two kinds of trees.
It lists problems and then solutions for farmers.
It tells a story about one gardener.
It follows water from the roots to the leaves, then tells why it matters.
questions.why: The article moves step by step from roots to stem to leaves, then explains how plants use water.

wrong.A: The article does not compare two kinds of trees.
wrong.B: The article is not organized as problems and solutions.
wrong.C: There is no story about a gardener.

MID.prompt: Imagine you are a drop of water. Describe your trip through a plant from the soil to the air. Use the words xylem and evaporate.
checklist: I described the trip in the correct order.
I used the words xylem and evaporate correctly.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
MID.modelAnswer: I start in the soil, where a root hair helps absorb me into the plant. Next, I travel upward through the xylem, like a thin straw running from the roots to the leaves. Inside a leaf, I turn into vapor and evaporate out through a tiny hole, and as I escape, I also carry minerals up with me for the plant to use.

keyWords.definition: tiny openings in a leaf that let gases and water vapor in and out
keyWords.example: Many stomata are on the underside of a leaf.

keyWords.definition: the loss of water as vapor from the leaves of a plant
keyWords.example: On a hot afternoon, transpiration makes a tree lose a lot of water.

keyWords.definition: the way particles of the same thing stick together
keyWords.example: Because of cohesion, drops of water on a window join into bigger drops.

keyWords.definition: the way plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make food
keyWords.example: Photosynthesis slows down when the days grow shorter.

keyWords.definition: water stored under the ground in soil and rock
keyWords.example: The farm's well brings up groundwater for the crops.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the central idea of the article?
options: Plants lose water mainly because of poor soil.
Roots absorb water, which transpiration and cohesion pull up the xylem to be used for food, minerals, and support.
Celery is the best plant for studying how water moves.
Botanists still have no idea how water climbs a tall tree.
questions.why: The article explains the whole path of water and why plants need it, which this choice sums up.

wrong.A: The article does not blame soil for water loss.
wrong.C: Celery is used only as one example of an experiment.
wrong.D: The article explains the answer scientists found, so this is false.

questions.stem: According to the article, what are stomata?
options: Hairs on roots that gather moisture
Tubes in the stem that carry water
Minerals that dissolve in water
Microscopic pores in leaves where vapor escapes
questions.why: The article says leaves contain tiny pores called stomata, and water vapor escapes through them.

wrong.C: Minerals are carried by water; they are not stomata.

questions.stem: What does the celery experiment show?
options: The path water takes up through the plant
That celery makes food faster in colored water
That food coloring helps plants grow
That water moves down from the leaves
questions.why: Colored streaks appear in the leaves, revealing the path the water followed through the xylem.

wrong.B: The experiment is not about making food.
wrong.C: The article does not say coloring helps growth.
wrong.D: The streaks show water moving up into the leaves, not down.

questions.stem: Why does one evaporating water molecule pull on the water below it?
options: Gravity pulls the molecule down into the roots.
The stomata pump each molecule up the stem.
Water molecules cling tightly to one another.
Minerals push the molecule toward the leaf.
questions.why: The article says water molecules cling together, a property called cohesion, so each one tugs on its neighbor.

wrong.A: Gravity works against the rising water, not with it.
wrong.D: The article does not say minerals push water upward.

questions.stem: If every stoma on a plant's leaves were sealed shut, what would most likely happen?
options: Water would rise faster than before.
Much less water would be pulled up from the roots.
The roots would grow many more hairs.
The plant would stop needing minerals.
questions.why: Transpiration through the stomata is what pulls water up, so closing them would weaken that pull.

wrong.A: Without evaporation from the leaves, the pull would weaken, not grow.
wrong.C: The article gives no reason to think roots would grow more hairs.
wrong.D: Plants still need minerals no matter what the stomata do.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin by pointing out that plants have no mouths?
options: To raise a puzzle that the rest of the article solves
To argue that plants are less alive than animals
To compare plants to animals in every paragraph
To show that plants never need to drink
questions.why: The opening makes readers wonder how water gets in, and the article then explains it step by step.

wrong.B: The author never argues that plants are less alive.
wrong.C: The article does not compare plants to animals throughout.
wrong.D: The article says every plant depends on water.

questions.stem: Read the phrase: "date palms flourish in arid regions." What does arid mean?
options: Cold and snowy
Crowded with people
Full of rivers
Very dry
questions.why: The palms need deep roots to reach groundwater, which shows the land has very little water, so arid means very dry.

wrong.A: The article describes desert land, not cold land.
wrong.B: Arid describes the land and weather, not people.
wrong.C: If the land were full of rivers, the palms would not need such deep roots.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why a wilting plant droops?
options: Its roots have grown too long.
Its leaves are making too much food.
Without enough water, its stems and leaves lose firmness.
Its stomata have filled with minerals.
questions.why: The article says water keeps stems and leaves firm, so losing water makes them go soft and droop.

wrong.A: Long roots help a plant find water; they do not cause drooping.
wrong.B: Making food does not cause drooping in the article.
wrong.D: The article does not say stomata fill with minerals.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how transpiration and cohesion work together to move water from a plant's roots to its leaves. Use details from the article to support your explanation.
checklist: I explained both transpiration and cohesion.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my explanation in clear, complete sentences.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Transpiration is the process in which water evaporates out through the stomata, the tiny holes in a leaf, and escaping this way pulls on the water molecules behind it. Because water molecules stick together through cohesion, that single tug is enough to drag an entire column of water up the xylem from the roots to the leaves. The article explains that once the water arrives, it supplies the plant with the moisture needed for photosynthesis, which shows how transpiration and cohesion work as one continuous pulling system.
